ai.definition: Neuromorphic processors are computing devices that mimic the structure and function of biological neural networks. They process information using spiking neurons and event-driven communication rather than traditional clocked pipelines.
ai.howItWorks: These chips contain many simple digital neuron cores that fire asynchronously, meaning they only consume power when active. This asynchronous firing allows for efficient computation with minimal energy consumption.
ai.problemSolved: They address the inefficiencies of traditional computing architectures by reducing idle power usage and enabling more efficient processing of complex data like sensory inputs or real-time decision-making tasks.
ai.manufacturing: Manufactured using advanced semiconductor fabrication techniques, typically involving multiple layers of transistors and interconnects to simulate synaptic connections in a biological brain.
ai.buildProcess: The process involves designing neuron cores, integrating them into a network architecture, and programming the chip to emulate neural behavior through spike-based communication and event-driven processing.
ai.costDrivers: High initial R&D costs for developing accurate models of neurons and synapses, specialized fabrication processes, and complex design verification.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: expected to transition into early commercialization with significant advancements in the coming years
ai.regulation: Currently no specific regulations but may require updates as they become more prevalent in critical applications like healthcare or autonomous vehicles.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving sufficient accuracy and reliability of neuron models, ensuring robustness against noise and interference. Market risks involve competition from traditional silicon vendors and the need to establish standards for neuromorphic systems.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to early stage but has potential in niche markets like IoT sensing and robotics where low power consumption is critical.
ai.futureDevelopment: Expected advancements include more accurate neuron models, integration with other AI techniques, and optimization of hardware-software co-design.

glossary.def: relating to or inspired by the structure and function of biological neural networks
artificial neuron models that fire (or 'spike') in response to input, mimicking biological neurons
a method where components communicate only when necessary, reducing power consumption compared to continuous clocked pipelines

subsystems.name: Neuron cores
subsystems.role: emulate spiking neuron dynamics — accumulating input, firing when a threshold is crossed, then resetting.

subsystems.name: Synapse crossbar
subsystems.role: store synaptic weights and compute the weighted sum of incoming spikes.
parts: resistive memory cells or SRAM cells

subsystems.name: Asynchronous router
subsystems.role: deliver spikes between cores only when they occur, with no global clock.

subsystems.name: Learning engine
subsystems.role: adjust weights locally according to spike timing, so the chip can adapt without a central controller.

subsystems.name: Sensor interface
subsystems.role: convert real-world signals into spike trains and send decisions back out.

subsystems.name: Power management
subsystems.role: keep idle circuits effectively off, so power scales with activity rather than clock speed.

buildSteps.title: Define the neuron model and network
buildSteps.detail: Choose the spiking neuron equations, connectivity and learning rule, then validate them in software simulation.

buildSteps.title: Map the network to hardware
buildSteps.detail: Assign neurons to cores and synapses to crossbar rows and columns, balancing fan-out against routing resources.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the silicon
buildSteps.detail: Use a standard CMOS process, often with extra metal layers for dense spike routing and, in some designs, integrated non-volatile memory for weights.

buildSteps.title: Build the synapse arrays
buildSteps.detail: Deposit and pattern resistive memory cells or SRAM cells, then form the crossbars that multiply spikes by weights and sum the currents.

buildSteps.title: Lay out the asynchronous router
buildSteps.detail: Design a network-on-chip with request-acknowledge handshaking so packets move at their own pace without a clock.

buildSteps.title: Add learning circuits
buildSteps.detail: Place local circuits that detect the relative timing of pre- and post-synaptic spikes and nudge the weight up or down.

buildSteps.title: Package and test
buildSteps.detail: Probe the chip for spike timing, power draw and cell-to-cell variability, then bin parts by how closely they match the simulated model.

buildSteps.title: Write the software stack
buildSteps.detail: Provide compilers, libraries and simulators that take a trained spiking network and map it onto the chip's cores and crossbars.

prerequisites.why: they output spikes directly, matching the processor's native input and avoiding a power-hungry conversion stage.
multiplying inside the memory array saves energy, but resistive memory cells still suffer from variability and drift.
event-driven networks-on-chip work in research chips but are not yet a standard, well-supported design block.
demonstrated in several research chips, but reliable long-term learning in commercial silicon remains hard.
frameworks exist, yet mapping real applications onto spiking hardware still needs expert tuning.

pathway.milestone: research chips and first commercial edge products, such as always-on keyword spotting in hearables.
pathway.unlocks: ultra-low-power sensing that runs for weeks on a coin cell.

pathway.milestone: open-source toolchains and common benchmarks, so developers can compare designs fairly.
pathway.unlocks: faster adoption in wearables, industrial monitoring and automotive sensing.

pathway.milestone: hybrid chips that combine neuromorphic cores with conventional digital accelerators on one die.
pathway.unlocks: real-time robotics and adaptive control, where low latency matters as much as low power.

pathway.milestone: commercial chips that learn continuously on-device using local plasticity.
pathway.unlocks: always-adaptive edge intelligence that personalises without sending data to the cloud.
